# Tern: the complete reference for LLMs

Generated by tools/llms.tn from docs/reference.md, docs/grammar.md, library/std/*.tn, and
example programs. Tern source files end in .tn. Check a program with
`tern check --json prog.tn` and run it with `tern run prog.tn`.
Programs marked `(rejected on purpose)` show mistakes the compiler refuses.

# Tern language reference

This is the complete reference for writing Tern programs. It is written so that a
reader who has never seen Tern (a person or an LLM) can write correct code on the first
try. Every ` ```tern ` block below is a complete program that the test suite
(`tern run tests/runner/main.tn -- docs`) compiles and runs; when an ` ```output ` block follows, the
program's output must match it exactly. So the examples here are known to work.

## 0. The short version

Tern looks like Python, but it is statically typed and compiled, and **every value is a
copy**: there are no references, pointers, `None`, classes, or exceptions.

The rules that differ most from Python:

1. Functions are `fn name(a: int, b: str) int:`. Every parameter needs a type. The return
   type comes after the `)` with no arrow (`-> int` is also accepted). No return type = returns nothing.
2. `x = 5` creates a variable. Its type is fixed from then on. `x: float = 0.0` states a type.
   There is no `let` or `var`, and there are no global variables. Top-level `const NAME = value`
   declares a constant (computed at compile time, or on first use when it calls a function).
3. The top level of a file may only contain `import`, `from ... import`, `struct`, `enum`,
   `const`, `fn`, `extern`, and `export fn`. The program starts at `fn main():`.
4. Types: `int` (64-bit), `float` (64-bit), `bool`, `str`, `[T]` (array), `{K: V}` (map),
   structs, enums, tuples `(int, str)`, `fn(int) str` (functions). `==` compares any of them
   (except functions) by value.
   Generics: `fn first[T](xs: [T]) T`, `struct Pair[A, B]`. No null: a value that may be
   missing is an `Option[T]` (`Some(x)` or `None`), a result that may fail a `Result[T, E]` (§9).
5. `true`, `false` (lowercase). Logic is `and`, `or`, `not`. Strings use double quotes only.
6. No implicit conversions: `1 + 2.0` is an error. Write `float(1) + 2.0` or `1 + int(2.0)`.
   `str + int` is an error: write `"n=" + str(n)` or `f"n={n}"`.
7. `/` on two ints is integer division (truncates toward zero). There is no `//`.
8. Parameters are read-only. To let a function change the caller's variable, declare the
   parameter `mut` and pass it with `&`: `fn inc(n: mut int)` is called as `inc(&x)`.
9. Assignment copies: after `b = a`, changing `b` never changes `a` (this includes arrays,
   maps, and structs; the copy is lazy, so it is cheap until one side is written).
10. `for i in 0..n:` loops over `0, 1, ..., n-1`. There is no `range()`.
11. Arrays: `xs.push(v)`, `xs.pop()`, `len(xs)`. `push` copies `v` into the array, like `=`
    (so `v` stays usable, and it moves for free when `v` isn't used again). There is no `append`, list comprehension,
    or negative index. Use `xs.sorted()`, `xs.reversed()`, `sum(xs)`, `xs.sort_by(fn(x) key)`,
    `xs.map(...)`, `xs.filter(...)`: each returns a new value and leaves `xs` alone.
12. Structs have no methods inside them. Write a function whose first parameter is the
    struct; then `p.area()` calls `area(p)`.
13. Your functions may share a builtin's name (`fn get(s: Store, id: int)`): a call uses
    yours when its first parameter fits the first argument, and the builtin otherwise. See §20.

A complete program:

```tern
struct Item:
    name: str
    price: float
    qty: int

fn total(items: [Item]) float:
    t = 0.0
    for it in items:
        t += it.price * float(it.qty)
    return t

fn main():
    items: [Item] = []
    items.push(Item("apple", 0.5, 4))
    items.push(Item(name="pear", price=0.75, qty=2))
    print(f"{len(items)} items, total {total(items)}")
    for i, it in items:
        print(i, it.name)
```

```output
2 items, total 3.5
0 apple
1 pear
```

## 1. Running programs

```text
tern run prog.tn             compile and run (needs clang)
tern run prog.tn -- a b      pass arguments (read them with os.args())
tern check prog.tn           type/safety check only; prints "prog.tn: ok"
tern check --json prog.tn    errors as JSON (for tools and agents)
tern test prog_test.tn       run the `test_*` functions (see the `testing` module, §16)
tern fmt prog.tn             reformat the file in place
tern build prog.tn -o prog   make a native binary
tern emit prog.tn            print the generated C
tern guide                   print this reference
tern guide strings           print only the sections about a topic
```

`check --json` prints `{"ok": true, "file": ...}` or `{"ok": false, "errors": [...]}`, where
each error is `{"file", "line", "message", "hint", "source"}` (`hint` is `null` when there is
none; `source` is the offending line).

Compile errors look like `prog.tn:12: error: <message>`, often followed by a
`hint:` line when the code looks like another language. All errors in a file are
reported at once. A runtime error (index out of bounds, missing map key, division by
zero, `pop()` on an empty array) prints `runtime error in f (prog.tn:N): <message>` to stderr
(`(util.tn, line N)` when it happened in another file), then the Tern functions it came
through (`  in util.helper <- run <- main`), and exits with status 2.

## 2. Lexical rules

- Comments start with `#` and run to the end of the line. There are no block comments or docstrings.
- Blocks are made by indentation after a `:`, like Python. Use 4 spaces. A block with one
  statement may go on the same line: `if x > 0: print(x)`.
- A line continues while a `(`, `[`, or `{` is open, or after a trailing `\`.
- No semicolons.
- Integers: `42`, `1_000_000`, hex `0xff`, binary `0b1010`, octal `0o17` (`_` may separate
  digits anywhere). A decimal literal must fit in an int (up to `9223372036854775807`); a hex,
  binary, or octal one may use all 64 bits, and above that value it is negative
  (`0xffff_ffff_ffff_ffff` is `-1`), which is handy for hash constants and masks. A literal
  that doesn't fit is a compile error.
- Floats: `1.0`, `0.5`, `1e9`, `2.5e-3`, `6.02E+23` (an exponent makes a float). A dot needs digits
  on both sides: not `1.` or `.5`.
- Strings: `"double quotes"`, on one line. Escapes: `\n \t \r \0 \" \\`; `\xNN` is one
  byte (`"\x01"`, `"\xff"`); `\u00e9` (four hex digits) and `\u{1F600}` (one to six) are a
  Unicode character, stored as UTF-8. A malformed `\x` or `\u` is a compile error. Any other
  backslash is kept as is: `"a\qb"` is the four bytes `a \ q b`.
- Multi-line strings: `"""` ... `"""` (and `f"""` ... `"""`) may span lines and take the same
  escapes; `"` needs no escape inside. When the text starts on the line after the opening
  `"""`, that line break and the one before the closing `"""` are dropped, and the indentation
  all its lines share is removed, so a block of SQL or HTML can be indented with the code.
- Raw strings: `` `C:\dir\file` `` between backticks: every character as written, no escapes,
  may span lines (a backtick can't appear inside). Good for regular expressions and JSON.
- F-strings: `f"x = {x}, next = {x + 1}"`. Any expression whose value is an `int`, `float`,
  `bool`, or `str` goes in `{}` (for an array, map, or struct, use `print(label, xs)` or
  `json.encode(xs)`); `{{` and `}}` are literal braces. No format specs (`{x:.2f}` is an error): use the `fmt` module,
  `f"{fmt.fixed(x, 2)}"` (§12).
- Names: letters, digits, `_`. Names starting with `_` are private to their module.
- Keywords: `and break const continue do elif else enum export extern false fn for from if
  import in mut not null or parallel pass return struct take true while`. `match` is a soft keyword, `type` is one at the top level (`type Name = T`), and `is` is one after an expression (`x is None`).

## 3. Variables and types

```tern
fn main():
    n = 10                  # int
    ratio = 0.25            # float
    ok = true               # bool
    name = "tern"           # str
    xs = [1, 2, 3]          # [int]
    ages = {"ada": 36}      # {str: int}
    empty: [str] = []       # an empty collection needs a type...
    later = []              # ...or gets it from its first use
    later.push(1.5)
    n = n + 1               # reassigning keeps the type
    print(n, ratio, ok, name, xs, ages, empty, later)
```

```output
11 0.25 true tern [1, 2, 3] {"ada": 36} [] [1.5]
```

- A variable is created by its first assignment and lives until the end of the block it was
  created in. Create it before an `if` if you need it after:

```tern
fn main():
    label = ""
    if 3 > 2:
        label = "big"
    else:
        label = "small"
    print(label)
```

```output
big
```

- There is no declaration without a value (`x: int` alone is an error); use `x = 0`.
- Constants go at the top level: `const NAME = value` or `const NAME: type = value`. A value
  made of literals, other such constants, and operators (including `a if c else b`) is an
  int, float, str, or bool computed when compiling; it can also be a `match` pattern. A
  constant can be used anywhere a value can, and from other modules (`config.PORT`,
  `from config import PORT`). There are no global variables: constants can't change, so
  every task can read them.
- Any other value (a function call, an array, a struct, a compiled regex, a `task.shared_map()`
  cache) is computed when the program first uses it, once, even if many tasks use it at the
  same moment, and kept: `const EMAIL = re.must("[^@ ]+@[^@ ]+")` compiles the pattern once
  for the whole program. Its type comes from the value (write it, `const X: [str] = []`, when
  it can't). It can't be a `match` pattern, and a value that needs itself is a runtime error.

```tern
const MAX_USERS = 100
const NAME = "tern"
const BANNER = NAME + " v2"
const MASK: int = (1 << 12) - 1
const LIMIT = MAX_USERS * 2 if MASK > 0 else 0

fn kind(n: int) str:
    match n:
        MAX_USERS:
            return "full"
        _:
            return "ok"

fn main():
    print(BANNER, LIMIT, MASK, kind(100), kind(7))
```

```output
tern v2 200 4095 full ok
```

```tern
import re
import task

const WORD = re.must("[a-z]+")
const STOP = ["the", "a", "of"]
const SEEN = task.shared_map()            # one cache for the whole program

fn words(s: str) int:
    n = 0
    for m in WORD.find_all(s):
        if not (m.text in STOP):
            SEEN.add_int(m.text, 1)
            n += 1
    return n

fn main():
    lines = ["the cat sat", "a cat of note"]
    parallel for i in 0..len(lines):
        words(lines[i])
    print(SEEN.get_int("cat"), SEEN.get_int("the"), len(STOP))
```

```output
2 0 3
```
- Types can't change: `x = 1` then `x = "a"` is an error.
- Type syntax: `int float bool str byte f32`, `bytes16` and `f32x4` (16 bytes / four f32s at once: std simd), `[int]`, `[[str]]`, `{str: int}`, `{int: [Point]}`, `(int, str)`,
  `Point`, `http.Request` (a type from a module), `fn(int, str) bool`, `fn(str)` (returns nothing), `ptr` (C pointer).
- Wrong type names from other languages are errors: `string`, `i32`, `i64`, `f64`,
  `list[int]`, `List<int>`, `dict`, `Vec<T>`. (`void` is accepted only as a return type,
  where it means the same as leaving the return type out.)
- Default values when you need one: `0`, `0.0`, `false`, `""`, `[]`, `{}`.

## 4. Operators

| Operator | Works on | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `+ - * /` | int with int, float with float | `/` on ints truncates toward zero: `7 / 2 == 3`, `-7 / 2 == -3` |
| `%` | int | sign follows the left side: `-7 % 3 == -1` |
| `+` | str with str | concatenation |
| `*` | str with int | repetition: `"ab" * 3` |
| `== !=` | any two values of the same type | structs, tuples, and enums field by field, arrays and maps element by element; not functions or task handles |
| `< <= > >=` | int, float, str | strings compare by bytes |
| `and or not` | bool | short-circuit |
| `in` | `x in xs` (array), `k in m` (map key), `"a" in s` (substring) | |
| `& \| ^` | int with int | bitwise and, or, xor (for bools, use `and` / `or`) |
| `<< >> >>>` | int with int | shifts: `>>` keeps the sign (arithmetic), `>>>` shifts in zeros (logical) |
| `+= -= *= /= %=` | same as the operator | also `&= \|= ^= <<= >>= >>>=`; no `++` or `--` |
| `-x` | int, float | |
| `~x` | int | bitwise not: `~x == -x - 1` |
| `&x` | a variable, field, or element | only as an argument to a `mut` parameter |
| `x is P` | an enum value | true if `x` is variant `P`: `o is None`, `r is Ok(_)`, `if o is Some(v):` (§9) |
| `x?` | an Option or a Result | the value in `Some` / `Ok`, else return the `None` / `Err` at once (§9) |

- Int arithmetic wraps on overflow (64-bit two's complement). Division or `%` by zero is a runtime error.
- A shift count must be 0 to 63: `1 << 64` is a compile error when the count is written as a
  number, and a runtime error otherwise. `<<` shifts bits out of the top (it wraps like `*`).
- Precedence, lowest first: `or`, `and`, comparisons and `in`, `|`, `^`, `&`, shifts, `+ -`,
  `* / %`, then the unary `-x`, `~x`, and `not x` (so write `not (a == b)`). As in Python (not C),
  `x & 4 == 4` means `(x & 4) == 4`.

```tern
fn fnv1a(s: str) int:                     # a 64-bit hash
    h = 0xcbf2_9ce4_8422_2325
    for c in s:
        h ^= c.byte(0)
        h *= 0x100_0000_01b3
    return h

fn main():
    flags = 0b0101
    flags |= 1 << 3                       # set bit 3
    print(flags, flags & 0b100 != 0, flags >> 1, ~0)
    print(-16 >> 2, -16 >>> 60, 0xff, 0o17, 1e3)
    print(fnv1a("tern"))
```

```output
13 true 6 -1
-4 15 255 15 1000.0
-440267618092719894
```
- `a if cond else b` is a conditional expression (as in Python; there is no `c ? a : b`). Only the
  chosen side is evaluated, both sides have the same type, and it binds loosest of all, so
  `x = n * 2 if n > 0 else 0` means `x = (n * 2) if n > 0 else 0`:

```tern
fn sign(n: int) str:
    return "negative" if n < 0 else "zero" if n == 0 else "positive"

fn main():
    xs = [3, -1, 0]
    print(xs.map(fn(x) sign(x)), [] if len(xs) > 5 else xs[..1])
```

```output
["positive", "negative", "zero"] [3]
```

- There is no `**` (use `math.pow`) or `//`.
- Mixing int and float is always an error; convert with `float(i)` or `int(f)` (truncates toward
  zero; NaN, infinities, and floats outside int's range are a runtime error).

## 5. Control flow

```tern
fn main():
    for i in 0..3:                  # 0, 1, 2 (end is exclusive; no step)
        print("i", i)
    xs = ["a", "b"]
    for x in xs:                    # elements
        print(x)
    for i, x in xs:                 # index and element
        print(i, x)
    m = {"one": 1, "two": 2}
    for k, v in m:                  # key and value, in insertion order
        print(k, v)
    n = 3
    while n > 0:                    # counting down: use while
        n -= 1
        if n == 1:
            continue
        print("n", n)
    x = 7
    if x < 5:
        print("small")
    elif x < 10:                    # `elif`, never `else if`
        print("medium")
    else:
        print("large")
    for i in 0..100:
        if i == 2:
            break
    if x > 0:
        pass                        # an empty block needs `pass`
```

```output
i 0
i 1
i 2
a
b
0 a
1 b
one 1
two 2
n 2
n 0
medium
```

- `for i in a..b` with `a >= b` runs zero times. To count down, use `while`.
- The loop variable can't be assigned, and the array or map being looped over can't be
  changed inside the loop. To change elements while looping, loop over indices:
  `for i in 0..len(xs): xs[i] = xs[i] * 2`.
- `match` is covered in §9. There is no `switch`, `try`, `with`, `goto`, or `do/while`.

## 6. Functions

```tern
fn add(a: int, b: int) int:
    return a + b

fn greet(name: str):                        # no return type: returns nothing
    print("hello " + name)

fn divmod(a: int, b: int, q: mut int, r: mut int):
    q = a / b                               # `mut` parameters write back to the caller
    r = a % b

fn main():
    greet("ada")
    q = 0
    r = 0
    divmod(17, 5, &q, &r)                   # `&` marks each argument that may change
    print(add(2, 3), q, r)
```

```output
hello ada
5 3 2
```

- Every parameter has a type. There are no default values, keyword arguments (named
  arguments are only for building structs), variadic parameters, or overloading.
- A function with a return type must end with a `return` on every path.
- Parameter modes:
  - default: read-only. Assigning to it, or calling `push` on it, is an error.
  - `mut`: the function may change it and the caller sees the change. The caller must write `&x`.
  - `take`: the value moves into the function (no copy). The caller can't use `x` afterwards
    (pass `copy(x)` to keep a copy).
- To return several values, return a tuple: `fn divmod(a: int, b: int) (int, int):` then
  `return q, r`, and the caller writes `q, r = divmod(7, 2)` (§7, Tuples).
- To report failure, return a `Result[T, E]` (`Ok(value)` or `Err(error)`), or an
  `Option[T]` when there's nothing to say about why (§9). There are no exceptions.
- Method syntax: `x.f(a, b)` is the same call as `f(x, a, b)`. If the first parameter is
  `mut`, write `x.f(...)` or `f(&x, ...)`. `x.f` also finds `f` in the module where `x`'s type
  is defined, so `d.exec(...)` calls `sqlite.exec(d, ...)`.
- Functions can be defined inside functions (they are closures, §13) and may recurse.
  Top-level functions may be called before they are defined.

## 7. Structs

```tern
struct Point:
    x, y: int                              # several fields of one type

struct Player:
    name: str
    pos: Point
    scores: [int]

fn dist(p: Point) int:                     # "methods" are plain functions
    return abs(p.x) + abs(p.y)

fn move(p: mut Player, dx: int):          # a "mutating method"
    p.pos.x += dx

fn main():
    a = Point(1, 2)                        # positional: fields in order
    b = Point(y=5, x=-3)                   # named: any order; every field is required
    pl = Player("zed", a, [])
    pl.scores.push(10)                     # nested fields and arrays change in place
    pl.move(4)                             # same as move(&pl, 4)
    c = a                                  # a copy
    c.x = 100
    print(a.x, c.x, b.dist(), pl)
```

```output
1 100 8 Player{name: "zed", pos: Point{x: 5, y: 2}, scores: [10]}
```

- All fields must be given when building a struct; there are no default field values.
  Write a constructor function if you want defaults: `fn new_player(name: str) Player:`.
- No `self`, no classes, no inheritance, no interfaces. `==` compares two structs field by
  field; when equality means something else, write `fn same_user(a: User, b: User) bool`.
- A struct may contain an array of itself (`kids: [Node]`) but not itself directly.
  For graphs, store nodes in an array and refer to them by index.
- `print` shows structs as `Name{field: value, ...}`.

### Tuples

A tuple is a fixed group of values of any types, written `(a, b)`; its type is written the
same way, `(int, str)`. It is a value like a struct whose fields have no names: read them
by position with `t.0`, `t.1`. Functions return several values as a tuple, and `a, b = ...`
unpacks one (each name on the left is a new variable, an existing one, a field or element,
or `_` to skip a value).

```tern
fn divmod(a: int, b: int) (int, int):
    return a / b, a % b                   # parentheses are optional after `return` and `=`

fn main():
    q, r = divmod(17, 5)
    print(q, r)
    t = divmod(9, 2)
    print(t, t.0, t.1)
    a = 1
    b = 2
    a, b = b, a                           # swap
    _, rest = divmod(7, 3)
    scores: [(str, int)] = [("ada", 3), ("bob", 5)]
    scores.push(("cy", 4))
    for s in scores:
        print(s.0, s.1)
    print(a, b, rest, scores[1])
```

```output
3 2
(4, 1) 4 1
ada 3
bob 5
cy 4
2 1 1 ("bob", 5)
```

- A tuple has two or more values; there is no one-value tuple. `t.0 = 5` changes one value.
- The number of names on the left of `a, b = ...` must match the tuple.
- Tuples can go anywhere a type can: in arrays, maps, struct fields, and function types.
- `print` shows `(1, "a")`, and `==` compares tuples value by value. Tuples can't be turned
  into JSON yet.

### Generics

Functions, structs, and enums can take type parameters in `[ ]` after their name. A use
with concrete types makes a version of the function or type for those types (like C++
templates or Rust): it runs exactly as fast as code written by hand for them.

```tern
struct Pair[A, B]:
    left: A
    right: B

enum Tree[T]:                             # recursive generic enums work too
    Leaf
    Node(l: Tree[T], v: T, r: Tree[T])

fn first[T](xs: [T]) T:
    return xs[0]

fn largest[T: Ord](xs: [T]) T:            # a constraint: T must support < and >
    best = xs[0]
    for x in xs:
        if x > best:
            best = x
    return best

fn map_all[A, B](xs: [A], f: fn(A) B) [B]:
    out: [B] = []
    for x in xs:
        out.push(f(x))
    return out

fn insert[T: Ord](t: Tree[T], v: T) Tree[T]:
    match t:
        Leaf:
            return Tree.Node(Tree[T].Leaf, v, Tree[T].Leaf)
        Node(l, x, r):
            if v < x:
                return Tree.Node(insert(l, v), x, r)
            return Tree.Node(l, x, insert(r, v))

fn main():
    print(first([3, 1]), first(["a"]), largest([2.5, 9.0]))
    p = Pair(1, "one")                    # Pair[int, str], from the values
    q: Pair[str, [int]] = Pair("n", [])   # the declared type fills in [int]
    print(p, q, map_all([1, 2], fn(x) x * 10), first[str](["z"]))
    t = Tree[int].Leaf                    # explicit type arguments
    for v in [5, 2, 8]:
        t = insert(t, v)
    print(t)
```

```output
3 a 9.0
Pair{left: 1, right: "one"} Pair{left: "n", right: []} [10, 20] z
Tree.Node(l: Tree.Node(l: Tree.Leaf, v: 2, r: Tree.Leaf), v: 5, r: Tree.Node(l: Tree.Leaf, v: 8, r: Tree.Leaf))
```

- Type arguments are usually inferred: from the arguments, then from the type the result
  is going into (a typed variable, a `return`, a parameter), then from lambdas. When they
  can't be, write them: `first[int](xs)`, `Pair[int, str](1, "a")`, `Tree[int].Leaf`.
- A generic type always needs its arguments where a type is written: `Pair[int, str]`, not `Pair`.
- Constraints: `T: Ord` (int, float, str: `<`, `>`, sorting), `T: Eq` (`==`), `T: Hash`
  (usable as a map key); several: `T: Ord + Hash`. Without a constraint any type is
  accepted, and the body is checked for each type it is used with; an error there names
  the version, e.g. ``(in `total[Point]`, used on line 12)``.
- A generic function used as a value needs its arguments: `f = first[int]`.
- There are no traits or interfaces: pass behavior as a function value (`fn(T, T) bool`).

### Type aliases

`type Name = T` at the top level of a module gives a type a second name. The alias *is* the
type: values pass freely between the two names, `Name(...)` constructs one, and `x.f()` finds
`f` in the module that defines the original. A package uses aliases to present types that
live elsewhere under its own name (`roost.Request` is `http.Request`).

```tern
struct Point:
    x: int
    y: int

type Pos = Point
type Path = [Pos]
type Scores = {str: int}

fn walk(p: Path) int:
    total = 0
    for q in p:
        total += abs(q.x) + abs(q.y)
    return total

fn main():
    a = Pos(3, -4)
    b: Point = a                       # the same type under two names
    s: Scores = {"ada": walk([a, b])}
    print(a, s)
```

```output
Point{x: 3, y: -4} {"ada": 14}
```

- The alias's target is resolved in the alias's own module, so `type Request = http.Request`
  needs `import http` there; users of the alias don't.
- An alias can name any type (`[T]`, `{K: V}`, `fn(int) str`, another alias), but not
  itself, directly or through other aliases.
- Errors and printed values use the original name (`Point` above).
- `type` is a soft keyword: only `type NAME =` at the top level declares an alias, so `type`
  still works as a field or variable name.

## 8. Arrays `[T]`

```tern
fn main():
    xs = [3, 1, 2]
    xs.push(5)                     # append at the end
    last = xs.pop()                # remove and return the last element
    print(xs, last, len(xs), xs[0])
    xs[0] = 30
    zeros = [0] * 4                # [value] * n
    grid = [[0] * 3] * 2           # 2 rows of 3 (each row is its own copy)
    grid[1][2] = 7
    print(zeros, grid)
    print(xs[1..], xs[..2], xs[1..2], 2 in xs)   # slices are copies
    ys = xs.sort_by(fn(x) x)       # returns a new sorted array (stable)
    down = xs.sort_by(fn(x) -x)    # descending: negate a number key
    evens = [1, 2, 3, 4].filter(fn(x) x % 2 == 0)
    squares = [1, 2, 3].map(fn(x) x * x)
    print(ys, down, evens, squares, xs)
    print(xs.sorted(), xs.reversed(), sum(xs), sum([0.5, 0.25]), max(xs), xs.min())
    words = ["pear", "fig"]
    print(words.sorted(), words.sort_by(fn(w) len(w)))
```

```output
[3, 1, 2] 5 3 3
[0, 0, 0, 0] [[0, 0, 0], [0, 0, 7]]
[1, 2] [30, 1] [1] true
[1, 2, 30] [30, 2, 1] [2, 4] [1, 4, 9] [30, 1, 2]
[1, 2, 30] [2, 1, 30] 33 0.75 30 1
["fig", "pear"] ["fig", "pear"]
```

- `xs.extend(ys)` pushes every element of `ys` onto `xs`.
- Slices clamp to the length (`[1, 2, 3][1..10]` is `[2, 3]`), for strings too.
- Indexes start at 0. Out-of-range indexes are runtime errors. There are no negative
  indexes: the last element is `xs[len(xs) - 1]`.
- `xs.sorted()` is a sorted copy of an array of ints, floats, or strs; `xs.reversed()` is a
  copy in reverse order; `sum(xs)` adds an `[int]` or `[float]` (0 when empty; int sums wrap
  like `+`), and `min(xs)`, `max(xs)` find its smallest and largest (an empty array is a
  runtime error). None of them changes `xs`: to sort in place, write `xs = xs.sorted()`.
- `sort_by(xs, key)` sorts by a key that is an `int`, `float`, or `str` (stable). It never
  changes `xs`; it returns a new array. Descending: `xs.sort_by(fn(x) -x)` for numbers,
  `xs.sorted().reversed()` for strings.
- Other operations you might expect are short loops: `index_of`, `insert`, `zip`.
  Example: `for i in 0..len(xs): if xs[i] == v: return i`.
- Removing from the middle: build a new array with `filter`, or with a loop.
- `push` copies its value into the array the way `=` does: lazily, and not at all when the
  pushed variable isn't used afterwards (then the value moves).

```tern
fn main():
    names: [str] = []
    name = "ada"
    names.push(name)               # `name` is still usable
    name += "!"                    # and changing it doesn't change the array
    names.push("bob")
    print(name, names)
```

```output
ada! ["ada", "bob"]
```

- `copy(x)` makes an explicit copy. It is only needed for `take` parameters (§6).

### Bytes

`byte` is a number from 0 to 255, for binary data: pixels, network buffers, hashes. A `[byte]`
stores one byte per element (an `[int]` uses eight), so a 1024x1024 RGBA image is 4MB.

```tern
fn main():
    px: [byte] = [255, 128, 0, 64]      # a number 0-255 is a byte where one is expected
    gray = (px[0] * 77 + px[1] * 150 + px[2] * 29) >> 8    # bytes in arithmetic are ints
    out = [byte(0)] * 3
    out[0] = byte(gray)                 # storing an int takes byte(n): its low 8 bits
    out[1] = byte(300)
    out[2] = 250
    out[2] += 10                        # op= on a byte wraps
    data = "Tern".to_bytes()            # str <-> [byte] share memory: no copy
    data[0] = 116
    print(gray, out, data.to_str(), int(px[1]) * 2)
```

```output
151 [151, 44, 4] tern 256
```

- In arithmetic and comparisons a byte counts as an `int`, and so does the result:
  `px[0] * 77` can't overflow. `-b` is an int too.
- Storing an int into a byte (a variable, element, field, or argument) takes `byte(n)`, which
  keeps the low 8 bits. A literal from 0 to 255 needs no conversion; one outside that range
  is an error. `b += n` (any `op=`) on a byte wraps, as `byte(b + n)` would.
- `int(b)` and `float(b)` convert back. `s.byte(i)` still returns an `int`.
- `s.to_bytes()` gives a string's bytes, `bs.to_str()` makes a string of them. Both share
  the block (a `str` and a `[byte]` are laid out the same); writing to either copies it first.
- `print` and `json.encode` show bytes as numbers; `json.decode` rejects numbers outside 0-255.

### 32-bit floats

`f32` is a 32-bit float, for big arrays of numbers: vectors, embeddings, audio, model weights.
An `[f32]` stores 4 bytes per element (a `[float]` uses eight), so a million 768-number
embeddings take 3GB instead of 6GB. `std simd` works on four of them at once (`f32x4`), and
`std binary` reads and writes them as raw bytes (`binary.f32s_le`, `binary.f16s_le`).

```tern
fn dot(a: [f32], b: [f32]) f32:
    s: f32 = 0.0                        # a float literal is an f32 where one is expected
    for i in 0..len(a):
        s += a[i] * b[i]                # f32 * f32 is an f32
    return s

fn main():
    xs: [f32] = [0.5, 1.5, -2.0]
    ys = [f32(1), f32(2), 0.25 * xs[0]] # f32(n) converts an int or a float
    d = dot(xs, ys)
    print(d, float(d) * 2.0, xs.sorted(), sum(xs), f32(0.1), float(f32(0.1)))
```

```output
3.25 6.5 [-2.0, 0.5, 1.5] 0.0 0.1 0.10000000149011612
```

- Math on f32s stays in f32, as in Rust, Go and C. An f32 and a float don't mix: write
  `f32(x)` or `float(x)` (a literal like `0.5` adapts by itself).
- `print`, `str` and f-strings show the shortest decimal that reads back as the same f32
  (`0.1`, not `0.10000000149011612`); `json.encode` writes the same, and `json.decode` rounds.
- `int(x)`, `abs`, `sqrt`, `min`, `max`, `sum`, `sorted` and `sort_by` keys take f32s. An f32
  can't be a map key (nor can a float).
- In an `extern` block an f32 is a C `float`, and an `[f32]` a `float*`.

## 9. Enums and `match`

```tern
import math

enum Shape:
    Circle(radius: float)
    Rect(w: float, h: float)
    Empty

enum Expr:                                   # recursive enums just work
    Num(v: int)
    Add(l: Expr, r: Expr)

fn area(s: Shape) float:
    match s:
        Circle(r):                           # bind payload values by position
            return math.pi() * r * r
        Rect(w, h):
            return w * h
        Empty:
            return 0.0

fn eval(e: Expr) int:
    match e:
        Num(v):
            return v
        Add(l, r):
            return eval(l) + eval(r)

fn describe(code: int) str:
    match code:                              # match on int, str, or bool literals
        200:
            return "ok"
        404:
            return "not found"
        301 | 302 | 307:                     # several patterns, one arm
            return "redirect"
        _:                                   # `_` matches anything else
            return "other"

fn main():
    shapes = [Shape.Circle(1.0), Shape.Rect(w=2.0, h=3.0), Shape.Empty]
    for s in shapes:
        print(area(s))
    print(eval(Expr.Add(Expr.Num(2), Expr.Num(3))), describe(404))
    print(shapes[2])
```

```output
3.141592653589793
6.0
0.0
5 not found
Shape.Empty
```

- Build variants as `Enum.Variant(values)` or `Enum.Variant`. In patterns, write the bare
  variant name (`Circle(r)`) or `Shape.Circle(r)`; `_` ignores one value (`Rect(w, _)`).
  An enum from another module is named through it: `json.Value.Null`, or just `json.Null`
  when only one of the module's enums has that variant (both in patterns too).
- A `match` must handle every value: on an enum, every variant (or end with `_:`; missing
  variants are listed in the error); on an int or str, it needs a `_:` arm (`_: pass` when
  nothing should happen); on a bool, `true` and `false` or `_:`.
- Enum payloads can only be read with `match` (no `s.radius`). Enums without payloads can
  be compared with `==`.
- Each arm is a block; there is no fallthrough and no `case` keyword, and no guards (`if` inside arm bodies instead).
  Patterns that share a body are joined with `|`: `"cat" | "dog":`, `Dot | Point:` (variants
  that bind names each need their own arm).
- `x is Pattern` tests which variant `x` is: `if s is Circle(r):` (see Option below).

### Option and Result

Two generic enums are always available, without an import:

```text
enum Option[T]:            enum Result[T, E]:
    Some(value: T)             Ok(value: T)
    None                       Err(error: E)
```

`Option[T]` is a value that may be missing (Tern has no null); `Result[T, E]` is a result or
an error (Tern has no exceptions). Build them bare: `Some(3)`, `None`, `Ok(v)`, `Err("bad")`.
Test them with `match`, or with `x is Pattern`, whose names are bound in the `if` or `while`
block. And `x?` gives the value inside `Some` / `Ok`, or else returns the `None` / `Err` from
the function at once (the function must return an Option, or a Result with the same error type).

```tern
struct User:
    name: str
    age: int

fn find_user(us: [User], name: str) Option[User]:
    for u in us:
        if u.name == name:
            return Some(u)
    return None

fn parse_age(s: str) Result[int, str]:
    n = s.to_int(-1)
    if n < 0:
        return Err(f"bad age: {s}")
    return Ok(n)

fn total_age(texts: [str]) Result[int, str]:
    t = 0
    for s in texts:
        t += parse_age(s)?                  # an Err returns from total_age right here
    return Ok(t)

fn main():
    us = [User("ada", 36), User("bob", 25)]
    if find_user(us, "bob") is Some(u) and u.age > 20:
        print(u.name, u.age)
    match find_user(us, "zed"):
        Some(u):
            print("found", u.name)
        None:
            print("no zed")
    print(total_age(["1", "2"]), total_age(["1", "x"]))
    print(parse_age("7").unwrap_or(0), parse_age("?").unwrap_or(0), find_user(us, "q").is_none())
    cur: Option[int] = Some(3)
    while cur is Some(n):                   # a loop that runs while there is a value
        cur = Some(n - 1) if n > 1 else None
    print(cur)
```

```output
bob 25
no zed
Ok(3) Err("bad age: x")
7 0 true
None
```

- Methods: `o.unwrap_or(default)`, `o.unwrap()` (a runtime error on None), `o.expect(msg)`,
  `o.is_some()`, `o.is_none()`; on a Result: `r.unwrap_or(default)`, `r.unwrap()`,
  `r.expect(msg)`, `r.is_ok()`, `r.is_err()`, `r.ok()` (an Option of the value), `r.err()`.
- `None` needs to know its type: from a typed variable (`x: Option[int] = None`), a return
  type, or a parameter. Otherwise write `Option[int].None`.
- `x is V(a, b)` binds `a` and `b` only as the condition of an `if` / `while`, or on the
  left of `and` there (`if o is Some(v) and v > 0:`). Anywhere else it's a plain test:
  `x is None`, `r is Ok(_)`. There's no `is not`: write `not (x is None)`.
- `is` works on every enum, not just these two. A module can define its own `Option`,
  `Some`, and so on; its own names win.
- `r.context("loading config")` turns an `Err(e)` into `Err("loading config: " + e)` (for a
  `Result[T, str]`), `r.map_err(f)` transforms the error, and `o.ok_or(err)` turns an Option
  into a Result.
- `panic(msg)` stops with a runtime error on purpose (for "can't happen"), and
  `assert(cond, msg)` does when `cond` is false; the message is built only then. Like any
  runtime error, a `panic` in a task is raised again by `h.join()`, and one in a web handler
  answers 500. A function ending in `panic(...)` needs no `return` after it.
- `main` may return a `Result[int, str]`: `Err(msg)` prints `error: msg` and exits with
  status 1, `Ok(n)` exits with status `n`. So `?` works in `main` too:

```tern
import fs

fn read_port(path: str) Result[int, str]:
    text = fs.try_read(path).context("reading " + path)?
    n = text.trim().to_int(-1)
    assert(n != 0, "port 0 is reserved")
    if n < 0:
        return Err(f"not a port: {text.trim()}")
    return Ok(n)

fn main() Result[int, str]:
    fs.write("/tmp/tern_port.txt", "8080\n")
    port = read_port("/tmp/tern_port.txt")?
    print("port", port, read_port("/tmp/missing.txt").is_err())
    return Ok(0)
```

```output
port 8080 true
```

## 10. Strings `str`

Strings are UTF-8 bytes. `len`, indexing, and slicing count **bytes**, and `s[i]` is a
one-byte `str`. For ASCII text this is the same as characters.

```tern
fn main():
    s = "Hello, World"
    print(len(s), s[0], s[7..], s[..5], s[7..9])
    print(s.find("o"), s.find("zz"), s.contains("World"), "World" in s)
    print(s.starts_with("He"), s.ends_with("!"), s.upper(), s.lower())
    print(s.replace("l", "L"), "  pad  ".trim(), "ab".repeat(3), "ab" * 2)
    parts = "a,b,,c".split(",")
    print(parts, len(parts), "-".join(parts))
    print("42".to_int(0), "x".to_int(-1), "2.5".to_float(0.0), str(42) + str(2.5) + str(true))
    print(s.byte(0), chr(72), "b" > "a")
    out = ""
    for ch in "abc":                     # one byte at a time
        out = ch + out
    print(out, f"{s.lower()}: {len(s) * 2}")
```

```output
12 H World Hello Wo
4 -1 true true
true false HELLO, WORLD hello, world
HeLLo, WorLd pad ababab abab
["a", "b", "", "c"] 4 a-b--c
42 -1 2.5 422.5true
72 H true
cba hello, world: 24
```

| Function | Result |
|---|---|
| `len(s)` / `s.len()` | length in bytes |
| `s[i]`, `s[a..b]`, `s[a..]`, `s[..b]` | one-byte string, substring |
| `s.find(sub)` | index of the first match, or `-1` |
| `s.find_from(sub, start)` | the first match at or after `start`, or `-1` |
| `s.strip_prefix(p)`, `s.strip_suffix(p)` | `s` without `p` at its start / end (`s` itself if it isn't there) |
| `s.contains(sub)`, `sub in s` | bool |
| `s.starts_with(p)`, `s.ends_with(p)` | bool |
| `s.replace(old, new)` | every occurrence replaced |
| `s.trim()` | without leading/trailing whitespace |
| `s.upper()`, `s.lower()` | ASCII case change |
| `s.split(sep)` | `[str]` (empty pieces kept) |
| `sep.join(parts)` | `str` (called on the separator, like Python) |
| `s.to_int(default)`, `s.to_float(default)` | parsed number, or `default` if `s` isn't one (`to_int` doesn't allow spaces, and a number outside the int range gives `default`; `to_float` allows leading spaces) |
| `s.byte(i)` | the byte at `i` as an `int` |
| `s.reserve(n)` | room for `n` more bytes (`s` is changed: a `mut` place), so building a long string by `+=` doesn't grow and copy it on the way |
| `s.repeat(n)`, `s * n` | repeated |
| `str(x)` | `x` must be int, float, bool, or str |
| `chr(n)` | one-byte string from a byte value (0 to 255; anything else is a runtime error) |

- Strings are immutable values: `s[0] = "x"` is an error; build a new string instead.
- `int("42")` is an error (`int()` converts floats). Use `"42".to_int(0)`.
- `str()` of an array or struct is an error; `print` shows any value, and `json.encode` makes text from any value.
- Building a big string in a loop with `+=` is fine (it grows in place).

### Multi-line and raw strings

```tern
fn main():
    user = "ada"
    sql = """
        SELECT id, name
        FROM users
        WHERE name = $1
        """
    page = f"""
        <h1>Hello, {user}</h1>
        <p class="note">{len(sql)} bytes of SQL</p>
        """
    pattern = `^\d{3}-\d{4}$`
    body = `{"name": "ada", "tags": ["a", "b"]}`
    print(sql)
    print(page)
    print(pattern, body)
```

```output
SELECT id, name
FROM users
WHERE name = $1
<h1>Hello, ada</h1>
<p class="note">42 bytes of SQL</p>
^\d{3}-\d{4}$ {"name": "ada", "tags": ["a", "b"]}
```

- `"""` strings drop the line break after the opening quotes and before the closing ones,
  and the indentation their lines share: indent them with the code.
- `` `raw` `` strings keep every character: `\d` is a backslash and a `d`, handy for `re`
  patterns, JSON, and Windows paths. They have no escapes, so they can't hold a backtick.

## 11. Maps `{K: V}`

Keys are `int`, `str`, `bool`, or structs, enums, tuples, and arrays made of those (so not
`float` or functions): `{(int, int): str}` for a grid, `{Point: bool}` for a set of points.
Iteration order is insertion order.

```tern
fn main():
    ages = {"ada": 36, "bob": 25}
    ages["cy"] = 41                     # insert or overwrite
    ages["bob"] += 1
    print(ages["ada"], "bob" in ages, ages.get("zed", -1), len(ages))
    ages.remove("ada")
    print(ages.keys(), ages.values(), ages)
    counts: {str: int} = {}
    for w in "a b a c a".split(" "):
        counts[w] = counts.get(w, 0) + 1
    print(counts)
    groups: {int: [str]} = {}
    for w in ["hi", "yo", "hey"]:
        if not (len(w) in groups):
            groups[len(w)] = []
        groups[len(w)].push(w)
    print(groups)
```

```output
36 true -1 3
["bob", "cy"] [26, 41] {"bob": 26, "cy": 41}
{"a": 3, "b": 1, "c": 1}
{2: ["hi", "yo"], 3: ["hey"]}
```

- Reading a missing key with `m[k]` is a runtime error; use `k in m` or `m.get(k, default)`.
- `m.remove(k)` does nothing if `k` is missing. `m.keys()` and `m.values()` return arrays.
- `for k, v in m:` loops over pairs; `for k in m:` loops over keys.
- Write `not (k in m)` with the parentheses; there is no `not in` operator.
- A map can't be changed while looping over it. Loop over a copy of its keys instead:
  `for k in m.keys(): m[k] = 0`.

## 12. Printing

`print(a, b, ...)` prints its arguments separated by spaces, then a newline. It accepts any
value. Floats show a decimal point (`2.0`) and use the shortest exact form
(`0.1 + 0.2` prints `0.30000000000000004`); very large or small ones use exponent form (`1e+19`). Strings print raw at the top level and quoted
inside arrays, maps, and structs. There is no `end=` or `sep=`; build a string instead.

F-strings have no format specs. The `fmt` module does fixed decimals, padding, and digit grouping:

```tern
import fmt

fn main():
    price = 1234.5
    cents = 1205
    print(f"total: {fmt.fixed(price, 2)}, ${fmt.cents(cents)}, {fmt.thousands(1234567)}")
    print(fmt.zero_pad(7, 3), "[" + fmt.pad_left("ab", 5, " ") + "]", "[" + fmt.pad_right("ab", 5, ".") + "]")
```

```output
total: 1234.50, $12.05, 1,234,567
007 [   ab] [ab...]
```

## 13. Functions as values (closures)

```tern
struct Button:
    label: str
    on_click: fn(int) str

fn apply_twice(f: fn(int) int, x: int) int:
    return f(f(x))

fn make_adder(k: int) fn(int) int:
    return fn(x) x + k                   # a lambda: `fn(params) expression`

fn main():
    k = 10
    add = fn(x: int) x + k               # captures a copy of k now
    k = 99
    print(add(5), apply_twice(add, 1), make_adder(3)(4))
    b = Button("go", fn(n) f"clicked {n} times")
    print(b.on_click(2))
    fn fact(n: int) int:                 # a nested function: a multi-line closure
        if n <= 1:
            return 1
        return n * fact(n - 1)
    print(fact(5))
```

```output
15 21 7
clicked 2 times
120
```

- A lambda is `fn(params) expression`: one expression, no `:` and no `return`. For more than
  one line, define a nested `fn` and pass it by name.
- Parameter types may be left out when the context says them (a typed parameter, field,
  or variable, or `map`/`filter`/`sort_by`). Otherwise write them: `fn(x: int) x * 2`.
- A closure copies the variables it uses when it is created, and can't change them. To
  accumulate, loop instead, or use a `mut` parameter.

## 14. Values, `mut`, and the safety rules

Tern has no references, so aliasing bugs and data races are compile errors. The rules and
the fix for each:

| You wrote | Error says | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| `n += 1` where `n` is a parameter | can't modify parameter `n` | declare it `n: mut int` and call with `&x`, or return the new value |
| `inc(x)` where `inc` takes `mut` | write `&x` | `inc(&x)` |
| `swap(&a, &a)` or `f(&a, a)` | would see the same value twice | pass a copy: `b = a` then `f(&a, b)` |
| use of `xs` after `f(xs)` where `f` takes `take` | was handed to a `take` parameter | pass `copy(xs)` |
| `xs.push(...)` inside `for x in xs:` | can't modify `xs` while looping over it | `for i in 0..len(xs):`, or build a new array |
| two `parallel` tasks write one variable | data race | give each task its own variable, combine after the block |
| `parallel for` writes a shared total | would race | write `out[i]`, then sum `out` after the loop |

Within one expression, parts run left to right, and a compound assignment evaluates its target
once (`xs[f()] += 1` calls `f` once). Reading `x` and then passing `&x` to a call further
along the same expression (`print(x, bump(&x))`) is a compile error: save `x` first.

Copies are lazy (copy-on-write), so `b = a` is cheap; the copy happens when one of them is
written. And when `a` isn't used again, its value moves instead: `ys = xs; ys.push(v)` or
`xs = add(xs, v)` never copies, nor does `row = grid[i]; row[j] = 0; grid[i] = row`. `p = ps[i]` copies the element: to change the element itself, write `ps[i].x = 1`
or pass `&ps[i]` to a `mut` parameter.

```tern
struct Account:
    owner: str
    balance: int

fn deposit(a: mut Account, amount: int):
    a.balance += amount

fn main():
    accts = [Account("ada", 10), Account("bob", 0)]
    first = accts[0]              # a copy
    first.balance = 999           # changes only the copy
    deposit(&accts[1], 5)         # changes the element in the array
    accts[0].balance += 1         # so does this
    print(accts, first.balance)
```

```output
[Account{owner: "ada", balance: 11}, Account{owner: "bob", balance: 5}] 999
```

Copying ordinary data (numbers, strings, arrays, maps, structs, tuples, enums) makes an
independent value. A few types are *handles* to something outside the value: a channel,
a `task.shared`, a task, and resources such as an open file, a database, or a connection.
Copying a handle gives a second name for the same thing, so a change made through either
copy is seen through both:

```tern
import task

fn main():
    a = task.shared(0)
    b = a                         # the same shared value, not a copy of it
    fn bump(n: mut int):
        n += 1
    b.update(bump)
    print(a.get(), b.get())
```

```output
1 1
```

## 15. Parallelism

```tern
fn fib(n: int) int:
    if n < 2:
        return n
    return fib(n - 1) + fib(n - 2)

fn main():
    c = 0
    parallel:                         # each line is a task; waits for all of them
        a = fib(20)
        b = fib(21)
        do:                           # `do:` groups several lines into one task
            c = fib(5)
            c += 1
    print(a, b, c)
    xs = [0] * 8
    parallel for i in 0..len(xs):     # iterations run across all cores
        xs[i] = i * i                 # iteration i may only write xs[i]
    total = 0
    for x in xs:
        total += x
    print(xs, total)
```

```output
6765 10946 6
[0, 1, 4, 9, 16, 25, 36, 49] 140
```

- A variable created by a one-line task is visible after the block. Variables created
  inside a `do:` group are local to it; create them before the block to use them after.
- The compiler rejects any task that writes a variable another task reads or writes. One
  exception: tasks may write different elements of an array written with literal indexes
  (`xs[0] = a()` in one task, `xs[1] = b()` in another), if they don't touch the array otherwise.
- `parallel` needs no threads, locks, or channels. For long-running concurrent work
  (tasks that outlive a block, channels between them, shared state behind a lock), use the
  `task` module; its functions are listed at the top of `library/std/task.tn`.

Tasks (`import task`) are green threads, like Go's goroutines: code in a task looks
blocking, but only the task waits (`ch.recv()`, `h.join()`, `time.sleep`, socket reads),
and its core runs other tasks meanwhile. Copying a `chan`, `task`, or `shared` value
shares it. Values sent through a channel are copied (cheaply: copy-on-write).

```tern
import task

fn fetch(id: int) str:
    task.sleep(10)                    # parks this task only; others keep running
    return f"page {id}"

fn produce(ch: chan[int], n: int):
    for i in 1..n + 1:
        ch.send(i * i)
    ch.close()                        # ends the receiver's `for` loop

fn main():
    hs: [task[str]] = []
    for id in 0..3:
        hs.push(task.spawn(fn() fetch(id)))   # all three run at once
    for h in hs:
        print(h.join())               # waits; an error in the task is raised here

    ch: chan[int] = task.channel(8)   # holds up to 8 values (0: unbounded)
    task.spawn(fn() produce(ch, 5))
    total = 0
    for x in ch:                      # until closed and empty
        total += x
    print(total)

    hits = task.shared(0)             # shared[int]: many tasks, one value
    fn bump(n: mut int):
        n += 1
    ws: [task[void]] = []
    for i in 0..100:
        ws.push(task.spawn(fn() hits.update(bump)))   # one update at a time
    for w in ws:
        w.join()
    print(hits.get())
```

```output
page 0
page 1
page 2
55
100
```

- `task.spawn` takes a function with no parameters; wrap a call in a lambda to pass arguments.
  The task gets copies of what the lambda uses, as with any closure.
- A channel needs its type written: `ch: chan[int] = task.channel(8)`. `ch.recv()` on a
  closed, empty channel is a runtime error; `for x in ch:` and `ch.next(&x)` stop instead.
- A runtime error in a task ends that task; `h.join()` raises it again. Other tasks keep
  running. The program ends when `main` returns; if a task failed and nobody joined it, its
  error is printed and the program exits with status 2 (tasks spawned inside web handlers
  don't count). `h.cancel()` on a task that already failed discards its error.
- `task.local_set(key, value)`, `task.local_get(key) str` (`""` if unset) and
  `task.local_clear()` keep strings that belong to the running task (a request id, tracing
  context). A spawned task starts with a copy of its spawner's. `task.id() int` names the
  running task (0 outside tasks).
- `os.on_error(f)` calls `f(os.ErrorReport)` for every runtime error from then on, caught
  ones too (a failed task, a web handler's `500`): for error trackers. See [os](std/os.md).
- Code inside `parallel:` may use channels too; there it waits like a thread.

### Groups of tasks: `task.all`, `task.try_all` (Go's errgroup)

`task.all(fs)` runs every function in `fs` (`[fn() T]`) at once and returns their results in
order; a runtime error in one is raised in the caller. `task.try_all(fs)` does the same for
functions that return `Result[T, E]`: `Ok` with every value in order, or the first `Err` to
arrive, after cancelling the tasks still running. `task.try_all_limit(fs, n)` runs at most
`n` at a time (Go's `SetLimit`), for "fetch these 500 URLs, 8 at once".

```tern
import task

fn fetch(id: int) Result[str, str]:
    if id == 13:
        return Err(f"page {id}: not found")
    return Ok(f"page {id}")

fn main():
    print(task.all([fn() 2 + 2, fn() 3 * 3]))
    good: [fn() Result[str, str]] = []
    for id in 0..4:
        good.push(fn() fetch(id))
    print(task.try_all_limit(good, 2))
    bad: [fn() Result[str, str]] = [fn() fetch(1), fn() fetch(13)]
    print(task.try_all(bad))                  # the first Err; any still running are cancelled
```

```output
[4, 9]
Ok(["page 0", "page 1", "page 2", "page 3"])
Err("page 13: not found")
```

### Counters and caches: `task.atomic`, `task.shared_map`

`shared[T]` changes any value safely, but each `get` and `update` takes a lock that tasks
wait for in turn: fine for occasional changes, slow for a counter or cache that every request
touches. For those two cases there are faster handles (copies share one, like channels):

- `task.atomic(v)`: an `int` changed with atomic instructions. `a.load()`, `a.store(v)`,
  `a.add(n)` (returns the new value), `a.cas(old, new)` (stores `new` if the value was `old`).
- `task.shared_map()`: a `str -> str` map any task can use at once (`m.put(k, v)`,
  `m.get_or(k, default)`, `m.has(k)`, `m.remove(k)`, `m.count()`), plus an `int` per key for
  counting (`m.add_int(k, n)`, `m.get_int(k)`).

Under contention they are hundreds of times faster than `shared[T]`. Copies share the same one
(like a channel), and the last copy gone frees it, entries and all: a cache can start again
with a fresh map.

```tern
import task

fn visit(hits: task.Atomic, pages: task.SharedMap, path: str) int:
    pages.add_int(path, 1)
    return hits.add(1)

fn main():
    hits = task.atomic(0)
    pages = task.shared_map()
    pages.put("/", "home")
    hs: [task[int]] = []
    for i in 0..100:
        p = "/" if i % 2 == 0 else "/about"
        hs.push(task.spawn(fn() visit(hits, pages, p)))
    for h in hs:
        h.join()
    print(hits.load(), pages.get_int("/"), pages.get_int("/about"), pages.get_or("/", "?"))
```

```output
100 50 50 home
```

| `url` | URLs by Go's net/url rules: `parse(text) Result[Url, str]`, parts as methods (`u.scheme() user() password() host() port() path() raw_query() fragment() opaque()`, plus `escaped_path() escaped_fragment() raw_path() raw_fragment() force_query() omit_host()`), setters (`u.set_path(p)`, `set_host`, `set_port`, `set_raw_query`, `set_fragment`, `set_scheme`, `set_user`, `set_password`), `u.parts() Parts` / `build(p: Parts) Url` for several at once, `format(u) str`, `resolve(base, ref: Url) Url`, `join(base, ref: str) Result[str, str]`, `u.host_port()`, `u.request_uri()`, `u.query() Query`; `parse_query(raw) Result[Query, str]`, `new_query()`, `q.get(k) str`, `q.get_all(k) [str]`, `q.has(k)`, `q.add(k, v)`, `q.set(k, v)`, `q.remove(k)`, `encode_query(q) str`, `query_string(pairs: {str: str}) str`; `query_escape`/`query_unescape`, `path_escape`/`path_unescape` (unescapes return `Result`) |
| `binary` | Binary formats, bytes in a `str`: `writer() Writer` with `w.put_u8/u16be/u16le/u32be/u32le/u64be/u64le(v)`, `put_f32be/f32le/f64be/f64le(v)`, `put_uvarint(v)`, `put_varint(v)` (zigzag), `put_bytes(s)`, `len()`, `bytes() str`; `reader(data) Reader` with `r.read_u8()` ... `read_u64le()`, `read_i8/i16be/i16le/i32be/i32le()`, `read_f32be()` ... `read_f64le()`, `read_uvarint()`, `read_varint()`, `read_bytes(n)`, `skip(n)`, `has(n) bool`, `left() int`, `ok() bool`, `error() str` (a read that doesn't fit gives 0 and every later one too; the first problem is kept); at an offset: `u8(s, i)` ... `u64le(s, i)`, `i16be` ... `i32le`, `f32be` ... `f64le`, `set_u8(&s, i, v)` ... `set_f64le` (past the end: a runtime error); `uvarint_len(v)`, `varint_len(v)` |
| `toml` | TOML 1.0: `decode(text, &out) Result[int, str]` (fills a struct by field name, like `json.decode`), `parse(text) Result[json.Value, str]`, `encode(value) Result[str, str]` (a struct or map), `dump(v: json.Value) Result[str, str]`; dates and times are RFC 3339 strings; errors name the line |
| `path` | paths as text, `/`-separated (Go's `path` rules): `join(a, b) str`, `join_all(parts) str`, `resolve(base, p) str` (an absolute p wins), `clean(p) str`, `dir(p) str`, `base(p) str`, `split(p) (str, str)`, `ext(p) str` (`".gz"`; none for `.bashrc`), `stem(p) str`, `with_ext(p, ext) str`, `parts(p) [str]`, `is_abs(p) bool`, `abs(p) str`, `rel(base, target) Result[str, str]`, `matches(pattern, name) bool` (`* ? [a-z] [!a-z] \x`), `glob(pattern) [str]` (sorted; `**` is any number of directories; hidden names only for a piece starting with `.`) |
| `csv` | RFC 4180 CSV, like Go's `encoding/csv`. `parse(text)` (`Result[[[str]], str]`), `records(text)` (`Result[[{str: str}], str]`, the first row is the header), `reader(text) Reader` + `r.next(&row) bool` / `r.err` / `r.line` (one record at a time), `format(rows) str`, `format_row(row) str`; `options() Options` (`sep comment fields lazy_quotes trim_leading_space crlf`), `tsv()`, and `parse_with` / `records_with` / `reader_with` / `format_with` / `format_row_with` taking them; errors name the line and column |
| `html` | escaping and templates that escape by default. `escape(s) str`; `render(template, data_json) str`, `render_file(path, data_json) str` (parsed once, reloaded on change; `{{> file}}` includes); `error() str`; Result forms `try_render(template, data_json)`, `try_render_file(path, data_json)` (`Result[str, str]`). Tags: `{{x}}` `{{a.b}}` `{{.}}` escaped, `{{{x}}}` raw, `{{json x}}`, `{{#each xs}}..{{/each}}` with `{{@index}}`, `{{#if x}}..{{else}}..{{/if}}`, `{{#unless x}}`, `{{! comment}}`; data is `json.encode(value)` |
| `tls` | TLS (aws-lc, which `tern` builds once per target and links only when imported; `TERN_TLS=system` uses the system's OpenSSL); importing it also enables `https://` in `http.get/fetch` and `s.listen_tls(...)` / `roost.serve_tls(r, port, cert, key)` / `roost.start_tls(r, host, port, cert, key) Server`. `connect(host, port) net.Conn` (verified; `c.ok()`, else `tls.error()`), `connect_insecure(host, port)`, `upgrade(c, host) bool` (STARTTLS), `server(cert, key) Server`, `accept(c, s) bool`, `version(c) str`, `trust(ca_file) bool`; `dial(host, port) Result[net.Conn, str]`; ALPN: `set_alpn(s, protocols: [str])` (server, preferred first), `connect_alpn(host, port, protocols) net.Conn`, `alpn(c) str` (the protocol agreed, e.g. `"h2"`) |
| `testing` | `eq_int eq_float eq_str eq_bool (got, want)`, `eq_ints eq_strs`, `near(got, want, tol)`, `is_true(cond, what)`, `is_false`, `includes(s, sub)`, `fail(msg)`: checks for `tern test` ([cli.md](cli.md#testing)) |
| `queue` | client for the `ternq` broker (`examples/queue/`): `connect(host, port) Client`, `connect_many(["h1:7070,h2:7071"])` (shards; each with failover addresses), `connect_auth(addrs, token)`, `c.publish(q, body) bool`, `c.publish_batch`, `c.subscribe(q, group, prefetch) Sub`, `s.next(&m) bool`, `c.ack(m)`, `c.nack(m)`, `c.fetch(s, max)`, `c.fetch_wait(s, max, ms)`, `c.stats(q)`. See `library/queue/queue.tn` |
| `openapi` | OpenAPI 3.1 from web routes (package). `new(title, version, description) Spec`, `bearer(&s, desc)`, `server(&s, url)`; `op(method, path, summary) Op` then `o.returns[T]()`, `o.accepts[T]()`, `o.returns_text()`, `o.status(n)`, `o.query(name, type, desc)`, `o.describe(t)`, `o.tag(t)`, `o.id(t)`, `o.fails(code, desc)`, `o.public()`; `add(&s, &r, o, handler)` registers the route too, `record(&s, o)` only documents; `document(s) str`, `typescript(s) str` (types + `createClient`), `serve(s, &r)` (`/openapi.json`, `/docs`) |
| `pg` | PostgreSQL. `pool(url, size) Pool`, `connect(url) Pool`; `p.ok()`, `pg.error() str`; `p.exec(sql, params: [str]) int` (rows; -1 on error); `p.query(sql, params) [{str: str}]`; `p.query_json(sql, params) str` / `p.query_row_json(...)` (typed JSON for `json.decode(…, &structs)`); `p.begin()`, `p.commit()`, `p.rollback()` (transactions bound to the task); `p.stats() PoolStats` (size open idle in_use waiting waits wait_ms timeouts opened closed), `p.prune()`, `p.close()`; URL `&pool_timeout=30s&max_lifetime=1h&max_idle=30m&statement_cache=off&application_name=x`. Params are `$1, $2`; `?sslmode=require` needs `import tls`; `fetch[T](sql, params) Result[[T], str]`, `fetch_one[T](sql, params) Result[Option[T], str]`, `pg.NULL` (a NULL parameter), `array_int(xs)` / `array_float` / `array_bool` / `array_str` (a list as one parameter: `= ANY($1)`), rows fill `[int]` `[str]` ... fields from PostgreSQL arrays, `run(sql, params) Result[int, str]`, `run_script(sql) Result[int, str]` (several statements, simple protocol), `describe(sql) Result[Statement, str]` (param type names; columns: name type_name type_oid kind base_type table not_null); `Option` fields decode NULL as None |
| `redis` | Redis client (package). `connect(url) Client` / `pool(url, size)`; `c.ok()`, `redis.error()`; `c.get_str(k) str`, `c.set_str(k, v) bool`, `c.set_ex(k, v, secs)`, `c.set_nx(k, v)`, `c.del(k) int`, `c.exists(k) bool`, `c.incr(k) int`, `c.incr_by(k, n)`, `c.expire(k, secs)`, `c.ttl(k)`, `c.mget(keys) [str]`, `c.publish(ch, msg) int`; `c.cmd(args: [str]) Reply` (kind text num items), `c.pipeline([[str]]) [Reply]`; `c.subscribe(channels) Subscription`, `sub.next(&m) bool`, `sub.unsubscribe()`; `c.close()`; `c.try_get(k) Result[Option[str], str]`, `c.try_cmd(args) Result[Reply, str]` |
| `auth` | JWT HS256 and signed-cookie sessions (package). `jwt_for(subject, secret, ttl) str`, `jwt_encode(payload_json, secret) str`, `jwt_verify(token, secret) Token` (ok payload subject error), `require_jwt(secret)` middleware (ctx "jwt.sub"); `session(req, secret) {str: str}`, `set_session(&res, secret, data)`, `set_session_for(&res, secret, data, max_age, attrs)`, `clear_session(&res)`; `verify(token, secret) Result[Token, str]` |
| `migrate` | schema migrations (package) for PostgreSQL and SQLite from `VERSION_NAME.sql` files (`-- migrate:up`, `-- migrate:down`, `-- migrate:no-transaction`). `postgres(p) Target`, `sqlite(d) Target`, `open(url) Result[Target, str]`; `t.up(dir)`, `t.down(dir, n)` (`Result[[Migration], str]`: what ran), `t.status(dir) Result[[Status], str]` (state: applied pending changed missing); `load(dir)`, `parse(version, name, text)`, `t.apply(ms)`, `t.rollback(ms, n)`, `t.report(ms)`; `create(dir, name) Result[str, str]`; `cli(dir, url) Result[int, str]` (up, down [N], status, new NAME); `label(m)`, `label_of(s)`, `split_statements(sql) [str]`. Each migration runs in a transaction with its bookkeeping; runs are serialized (pg advisory lock); an edited applied migration is an error |
| `sqlgen` | typed functions from SQL (package), like sqlc: `-- name: get_user :one` (or `:many`, `:exec`) above each query, `@name` parameters (`@x:int` to give a type, `@x?` for an `Option` that may be NULL), `"col!"` / `"col?"` / `"n: int"` column notes. `cli(url) Result[int, str]` (`QUERIES.sql ... -o OUT.tn [--migrations DIR] [--check]`), `generate(dbase, files) Result[str, str]` with `postgres(p)` / `sqlite(d)`; writes a Row struct per query and `fn q(pool: pg.Pool, ...) Result[Option[Row] | [Row] | int, str]` (SQLite: `fn q(conn: sqlite.Db, ...) Option[Row] | [Row] | int`); nullable columns are `Option` |
| `grpc` | gRPC over HTTP/2, over TLS (ALPN `h2`) or cleartext (h2c) (package): unary calls, HPACK with Huffman, many streams per connection. `start(host, port, handler: fn(Call) Reply, options()) Server`, `start_tls(host, port, handler, options(), cert, key) Server`, `serve(port, handler)`, `port(s)`, `wait(s)`, `stop(s, drain_ms)` (GOAWAY, then drains); `Call` has `method` (`"/pkg.Service/Method"`), `metadata` `{str: str}`, `message` (the request's bytes), `encoding` (`"gzip"` when compressed; accepted ones in `Options.encodings`); reply with `ok(body)` or `fail(status, msg)` (`grpc.OK` ... `grpc.UNAUTHENTICATED`); `Options`: `max_message max_frame max_header_list max_streams stream_window conn_window header_table encodings`; client `call(host, port, method, metadata, message) Reply` (h2c), `call_tls(...)` (TLS, verified). Imports `tls`. No streaming RPCs |
| `sentry` | error reporting to Sentry (package). `options() Options` (release environment server_name sample_rate max_queue breadcrumbs timeout_ms scrub), `init(dsn, o) Client`; `c.ok()`, `c.error()`; `c.capture_message(msg, level) str`, `c.capture_error(r: os.ErrorReport) str`, `c.capture_result(r: Result[T, str]) str` (the event id); `install(c)` (every runtime error, via `os.on_error`), `middleware(c)` (request data and route); `set_tag(k, v)`, `set_extra(k, v)`, `set_user(id, email)`, `clear_scope()` (task-local); `c.flush(ms) bool`, `c.close()`, `c.sent()`, `c.dropped()` |

Errors in the Result forms read `<module>: <what>: <reason>` (`fs: read /tmp/x: no such file or directory`).
| `http` | `serve(port, handler)` / `serve(port, handler, app)` / `serve(port, handler, &app)`; `Request{method, path, raw_query, head, body, params, ctx, conn}`; `Response{status, content_type, body, headers, upgrade}`; `text(s) html(s) json(s) status(code, s) not_found() no_content() redirect(url) with_status(res, code)`; `req.query(name) req.queries() req.header(name) req.headers() req.cookie(name) req.form(name) req.parts() req.param(name) req.json(&v)`; `res.set_header(name, v) res.set_cookie(name, v) res.get_header(name)`; `new_request(method, target, body) Request`, `req.add_header(name, v)` (tests); `match(path, "/users/{id}", &params) bool`; engine: `new_server() Server`, `s.add_route(method, pattern, h, ws, sse, stream)`, `s.listen(host, port, fallback)` / `s.listen_tls(..., cert, key)`, `s.wait()`, `s.stop()`, `ws_upgrade`, `sse_open`, `static_file(dir, rel, req)`; client: `get(url) post(url, body, type) fetch(request(method, url))`, `fetch_max(cr, max_body)` (fails past max_body bytes; `Connection: close` in cr.headers keeps it out of the pool); idle pooled connections close after `TERN_HTTP_POOL_IDLE`=30 s, at most `TERN_HTTP_POOL_MAX`=512 wait in all, `try_get`, `try_fetch`, `failed(res)`; middleware helpers: `client_ip limiter request_id gzip metrics_text` |

Builtins (no import): `print len push pop copy abs min max sqrt float int str chr` and the
string, map, and array functions in §8 to §11. Two more for web code: `json_quote(s) str`
(`s` as a JSON string literal, quotes and escapes included: `json_quote("a\"b")` is `"a\"b"`
with the quotes) and `url_decode(s) str` (`%20` and `+` become spaces). `min`/`max` take two numbers of the same type.
`abs` takes an int or a float; `sqrt` takes a float (`sqrt(float(n))`).

```tern
import math
import json
import fs

struct Config:
    name: str
    workers: int
    tags: [str]

fn main():
    print(math.sqrt(16.0), math.floor(2.7), math.pow(2.0, 10.0), min(3, 4), max(1.5, 0.5))
    c = Config("svc", 4, ["a"])
    text = json.encode(c)
    print(text)
    back = Config("", 0, [])
    if json.decode(text, &back):
        print(back.workers)
    bad = Config("keep", 1, [])
    print(json.decode("{not json", &bad), bad.name)
    path = "/tmp/tern_doc_test.txt"
    fs.write(path, "line1\nline2\n")
    lines = fs.read(path).trim().split("\n")
    print(lines, fs.exists(path))
    fs.remove(path)
```

```output
4.0 2.0 1024.0 3 1.5
{"name":"svc","workers":4,"tags":["a"]}
4
false keep
["line1", "line2"] true
```

A web server with a database (build with `tern build app.tn -o app`):

```text
import http
import sqlite
import json

struct Todo:
    id: int
    title: str

fn handle(req: http.Request, d: sqlite.Db) http.Response:
    params: {str: str} = {}
    if req.method == "GET" and req.path == "/todos":
        todos: [Todo] = []
        d.query_into("SELECT id, title FROM todos", [], &todos)
        return http.json(json.encode(todos))
    if req.method == "POST" and http.match(req.path, "/todos/{title}", &params):
        id = d.exec("INSERT INTO todos (title) VALUES (?)", [params["title"]])
        return http.json(json.encode(Todo(id, params["title"])))
    return http.not_found()

fn main():
    d = sqlite.open("todos.db")
    d.exec("CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS todos (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, title TEXT)", [])
    http.serve(8080, handle, d)
```

- The handler is `fn(req: http.Request) http.Response`, or takes a second parameter `app`
  (shared read-only by all threads), or `app: mut App` with `http.serve(port, handle, &app)`
  (requests that change it run one at a time).
- A runtime error inside a handler becomes a 500 response; the server keeps running.
- SQL parameters are always strings (`[str(id)]`) and are bound safely.
- Each server thread opens its own connection, so `sqlite.open(":memory:")` gives every thread
  a separate, empty database. Servers need a file path.
- A `sqlite.Db` is a handle, so a read-only `d: sqlite.Db` parameter can still run `INSERT`s: the
  database is outside the program's values. "Read-only" is about Tern values only.

## 17. Modules and packages

Every `.tn` file is a module. `import models` looks in the standard library and the
first-party packages (`roost`, `queue`, `pg`), then for `models.tn` or `models/` (a directory of
`.tn` files forming one package) next to the main file, then in `deps/`. Use `models.User`, `models.load(...)`, or `from models import User, load`.
Names starting with `_` are private. Third-party packages are git repositories: list them in
a `tern.mod` file next to your program and run `tern get`, which vendors them into `deps/`,
where `import` finds them (see [cli.md](cli.md#packages)).

## 18. Other targets and C

- `--target wasm | ios | ios-sim | android`; `build --lib` makes a C library with a header
  from `export fn` functions; `--shared` makes a `.so`/`.dylib`. On wasm, `--lib` also writes
  a JavaScript loader. Wasm runs `parallel` sequentially; `sqlite` and `http` aren't available there.
- Calling C: an `extern "header.h":` block of `fn` signatures (see README.md, "Calling C").
  Only `int float bool str ptr [int] [float]` and functions of those cross the boundary.
  `ptr` is an opaque C pointer; `null` is the null pointer (`p: ptr = null`) and
  `p.is_null()` tests for it. `null` is only a `ptr`: other types have no null.
  A `str` result stops at the first NUL byte; for binary data, return a `ptr` and a length
  and copy it with `string_at(p, n) str` (see guides/c-interop.md).

## 19. What Tern does not have (and what to write instead)

| From another language | In Tern |
|---|---|
| `def f(x):`, `func`, `function`, `fun` | `fn f(x: int) int:` |
| `class`, methods, `self`, `impl`, interfaces, traits | `struct` + functions taking it first; `x.f()` calls `f(x)` |
| `let x`, `var x`, `const X`, `x := 1`, `auto` | `x = 1` |
| global variables | `const MAX_USERS = 100` for fixed values; `const CACHE = task.shared_map()` for a program-wide cache; pass a struct for other state that changes |
| `None`, `null`, `nil`, `Option<T>`, `T?` | `Option[T]`: `Some(x)` or `None` (§9) |
| exceptions, `try/except`, `throw` | return a `Result[T, E]`: `Ok(v)` or `Err(e)`; `r?` passes an Err up, `r.context("...")` adds where (§9) |
| `panic!`, `assert`, `raise RuntimeError` | `panic(msg)`, `assert(cond, msg)`: a runtime error (§9) |
| `if let Some(v) = x`, `x is not None` | `if x is Some(v):`, `not (x is None)` |
| generics, templates, `<T>` | `fn first[T](xs: [T]) T`, `struct Pair[A, B]` (§7, Generics) |
| `any`, `interface{}`, `object` | a type parameter, an enum of the cases, or a function value |
| `True`, `False` | `true`, `false` |
| `&&`, `\|\|`, `!` | `and`, `or`, `not` |
| `x++`, `x--` | `x += 1`, `x -= 1` |
| `c ? a : b` | `a if c else b` |
| `//`, `**` | `/` on ints; `math.pow(float, float)` |
| `range(n)`, `range(a, b)`, `enumerate(xs)` | `0..n`, `a..b`, `for i, x in xs:` |
| `xs.append(v)`, `xs.length`, `xs.size()` | `xs.push(v)`, `len(xs)` |
| `xs.sort()`, `xs.reverse()` (in place) | `xs = xs.sorted()`, `xs = xs.reversed()` (`sort_by(fn(x) key)` for another order) |
| `sum(xs)`, `zip(xs, ys)` | `sum(xs)` works; for zip, `for i in 0..len(xs):` and read `xs[i]`, `ys[i]` |
| `[f(x) for x in xs if p(x)]` | `xs.filter(fn(x) p(x)).map(fn(x) f(x))` |
| `lambda x: x + 1`, `x => x + 1`, `\|x\| x + 1` | `fn(x) x + 1` |
| `int("42")`, `parseInt`, `strconv.Atoi` | `"42".to_int(0)` |
| `str(xs)`, `toString()` of a struct | `json.encode(xs)`, or `print(xs)` |
| `f"{x:.2f}"`, `%` formatting, `.format()` | `f"{x}"`; `f"{fmt.fixed(x, 2)}"`, `fmt.zero_pad`, `fmt.pad_left` |
| `'single quotes'` | `"double quotes"`; `"""..."""` over several lines; `` `raw` `` with no escapes |
| `else if`, `switch`, `case` | `elif`, `match` |
| `do { } while`, `loop` | `while true:` + `break` |
| `print(x, end="")` | build the whole line in a string, then `print` it |
| `import std.math`, `use`, `#include` | `import math` |

## 20. Builtin names

These are the builtin functions:

```text
print len push pop chr copy float int sqrt abs sum min max str join split find contains
starts_with ends_with replace trim upper lower to_int to_float byte repeat get remove
keys values is_null string_at map filter sort_by reversed url_decode json_quote panic assert
to_bytes to_str reserve
```

A function of your own, in the program or in a module, may have one of these names. A call
`get(a, ...)` or `a.get(...)` goes to your `get` when its first parameter fits `a` and the
number of arguments matches; otherwise it goes to the builtin, so the builtin still works on
strings, arrays, and maps next to yours:

```tern
struct Store:
    names: [str]

fn get(s: Store, i: int) str:
    return s.names[i]

fn len(s: Store) int:
    return len(s.names)

fn main():
    st = Store(["ada", "bob"])
    ages = {"ada": 36}
    print(st.get(1), get(st, 0), len(st), ages.get("ada", 0), len("hey"))
```

```output
bob ada 2 36 3
```

When the first argument is itself of a builtin type (a string, number, array, or map),
a call that doesn't fit your function goes to the builtin; for any other type, the error
is about your function. Functions in an `extern` block and `export fn` functions can't
take a builtin's name, because C sees that name: rename an extern one with `= "c_name"`.

## 21. Idioms

```tern
struct Parsed:
    ok: bool
    value: int

fn parse_port(s: str) Parsed:          # failure without exceptions
    n = s.to_int(-1)
    if n < 1 or n > 65535:
        return Parsed(false, 0)
    return Parsed(true, n)

fn index_of(xs: [str], want: str) int:  # search
    for i, x in xs:
        if x == want:
            return i
    return -1

fn main():
    p = parse_port("8080")
    if p.ok:
        print("port", p.value)
    print(parse_port("x").ok, index_of(["a", "b"], "b"), reversed([1, 2, 3]), sum([4, 5]))
    csv = "name,age\nada,36\nbob,25"
    total = 0
    for i, line in csv.split("\n"):
        if i == 0:
            continue
        cols = line.split(",")
        total += cols[1].to_int(0)
    print("total age", total)
    stack: [int] = []
    stack.push(1)
    stack.push(2)
    top = stack.pop()
    queue = [1, 2, 3]
    head = queue[0]
    queue = queue[1..]                   # pop from the front
    print(top, stack, head, queue)
```

```output
port 8080
false 1 [3, 2, 1] 9
total age 61
2 [1] 1 [2, 3]
```

Graphs and trees that need links between nodes use indexes into an array:

```tern
struct Node:
    name: str
    edges: [int]                          # indexes into the nodes array

fn main():
    nodes = [Node("a", [1, 2]), Node("b", [2]), Node("c", [])]
    seen = [false] * len(nodes)
    todo = [0]
    order: [str] = []
    while len(todo) > 0:
        n = todo.pop()
        if seen[n]:
            continue
        seen[n] = true
        order.push(nodes[n].name)
        for e in nodes[n].edges:
            todo.push(e)
    print(order)
```

```output
["a", "c", "b"]
```

# Tern grammar

The exact syntax accepted by the compiler (`compiler/syntax/lexer.tn`,
`compiler/syntax/parser.tn`), in EBNF. `{ x }` means zero or more, `[ x ]` optional, `|`
alternatives, quoted text is literal.
For what the constructs mean, see [reference.md](reference.md).

## Tokens

```text
NEWLINE   end of a line (not inside ( ) [ ] { }, and not after a trailing `\`)
INDENT    a line indented more than the one before; DEDENT: less (must match an earlier level)
          (a tab counts as 4 spaces; blank lines and comment-only lines are ignored)
comment   "#" up to the end of the line
NAME      letter or "_", then letters, digits, "_"   (not a keyword)
INT       digit { digit | "_" }                       e.g. 42  1_000_000  (at most 9223372036854775807)
          | "0" ("x"|"X") hexdigit { hexdigit | "_" }  e.g. 0xff  (hex, binary, octal: up to 64 bits;
          | "0" ("b"|"B") bindigit { bindigit | "_" }       above the largest int they are negative)
          | "0" ("o"|"O") octdigit { octdigit | "_" }
FLOAT     INT [ "." digit { digit } ] [ exponent ]    with a "." or an exponent: 3.14  1e9  2.5e-3
exponent  ("e"|"E") [ "+" | "-" ] digit { digit }     (not "1." or ".5")
STR       '"' { char | escape } '"'                   one line; escapes \n \t \r \0 \" \\
                                                      \xHH (a byte), \uHHHH and \u{H..} (UTF-8)
          | '"""' { char | newline | escape } '"""'    over lines; drops a blank first and last line
                                                      and the indentation the lines share
          | "`" { char | newline } "`"                 raw: every character as written, no escapes
FSTR      'f"' { char | "{{" | "}}" | "{" expr "}" } '"'
          | 'f"""' ... '"""'                           an f-string over lines, like """
keywords  and break const continue do elif else enum export extern false fn for from if import
          in mut not null or parallel pass return struct take true while
soft      match (a keyword only at the start of a statement followed by an expression),
          is (only after an expression)
symbols   -> == != <= >= .. += -= *= /= %= &= |= ^= <<= >>= >>>= << >> >>>
          ( ) [ ] { } , : . = + - * / % < > & | ^ ~ ?
```

## Program

```text
program     = { import | struct | enum | alias | const | fn | "export" fn | extern | NEWLINE } EOF
alias       = "type" NAME "=" type NEWLINE                      ("type" is a soft keyword here)
import      = "import" NAME NEWLINE
            | "from" NAME "import" NAME { "," NAME } NEWLINE
struct      = "struct" NAME [ tparams ] ":" NEWLINE INDENT field_line { field_line } DEDENT
field_line  = NAME { "," NAME } ":" type NEWLINE
enum        = "enum" NAME [ tparams ] ":" NEWLINE INDENT variant { variant } DEDENT
variant     = NAME [ "(" [ NAME ":" type { "," NAME ":" type } ] ")" ] NEWLINE
const       = "const" NAME [ ":" type ] "=" expr NEWLINE           (int, float, str, or bool, computed
                                                                  from literals, constants, operators)
fn          = "fn" NAME [ tparams ] "(" [ param { "," param } ] ")" [ [ "->" ] type ] block
param       = NAME ":" [ "mut" | "take" ] type
tparams     = "[" tparam { "," tparam } "]"                  (generic: fn first[T], struct Pair[A, B])
tparam      = NAME [ ":" NAME { "+" NAME } ]                  (constraints: Eq, Ord, Hash)
extern      = "extern" [ STR ] { ( "source" | "link" ) STR } ":" NEWLINE
              INDENT { "fn" NAME "(" [ param { "," param } ] ")" [ type ] [ "=" STR ] NEWLINE } DEDENT
```

## Types

```text
type        = "int" | "float" | "bool" | "str" | "byte" | "ptr"
            | NAME [ "." NAME ] [ "[" type { "," type } "]" ]   (a struct or enum, maybe from a module:
                                                 http.Request; with type arguments: Pair[int, str])
            | "[" type "]"                         (array)
            | "{" type ":" type "}"                (map; keys: int, str, bool, or arrays, structs, enums,
                                                 tuples of those)
            | "(" type "," type { "," type } ")"   (tuple)
            | "fn" "(" [ fparam { "," fparam } ] ")" [ type ]    (function; no type = returns nothing)
fparam      = [ "mut" | "take" ] type
```

## Statements

```text
block       = ":" ( NEWLINE INDENT stmt { stmt } DEDENT | simple NEWLINE )
stmt        = if | while | for | parallel | match | "do" block | fn | simple NEWLINE
if          = "if" expr block { "elif" expr block } [ "else" block ]
while       = "while" expr block
for         = "for" NAME "in" expr ".." expr block              (range: start inclusive, end exclusive)
            | "for" NAME [ "," NAME ] "in" expr block             (array: element or index, element;
                                                                  map: key or key, value; str: bytes)
parallel    = "parallel" block                                   (each statement is a task; `do` groups)
            | "parallel" "for" NAME "in" expr ".." expr block
match       = "match" expr ":" NEWLINE INDENT arm { arm } DEDENT
arm         = pattern { "|" pattern } block                  (alternatives bind no names)
pattern     = "_" | INT | FLOAT | STR | "-" INT | "true" | "false"
            | NAME { "." NAME } [ "(" [ NAME { "," NAME } ] ")" ]    (variant; "_" skips a value)
simple      = "return" [ exprs ] | "break" | "continue" | "pass"
            | NAME ":" type "=" expr                              (typed declaration)
            | place "=" exprs                                     (declaration or assignment)
```
